extracted.intended_audience: essayists and writers of satire/humour; literate general public interested in writing/style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing witty, satirical essays and moralizing humour — covering voice, use of persona, preface practice, and techniques for vivid satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid egotism / talking of oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a hard and nice Subject for a Man to speak of himself ... Let the Tenour of his Discourse be what it will upon this Subject, it generally proceeds from Vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from excessive first-person self-discussion in writing and conversation; speaking constantly of oneself is usually vain and diminishes the author's effect. Examples and anti-patterns cited: Tully/Cicero's self-justifications, Montagne's frequent self-reference, and the modern practice of memoir-fashioning. Memoirs and perpetual first-person attention are singled out as common faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reference permitted under fictional persona
rubrics_metrics.description: In Works of Humour, especially when a Man writes under a fictitious Personage, the talking of one's self may give some Diversion; but I would advise every other Writer never to speak of himself, unless there be something very considerable in his Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: using a fictitious speaker/persona who is self-referential can be entertaining and appropriate in humour. Outside of that device, only use personal disclosure when the author's character materially contributes to the piece (i.e., has notable comic or rhetorical value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial preface disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of our modern Prefaces savour very strongly of the Egotism. Every insignificant Author fancies it of Importance to the World, to know that he writ his Book in the Country, that he did it to pass away some of his idle Hours, that it was published at the Importunity of Friends...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not burden prefaces with irrelevant personal details about where, why, or under what casual circumstances a work was written. Such information reads as self-important and provides little value to readers; prefaces should be purposeful, not vanity-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not appropriate old jests as your own
rubrics_metrics.description: I mean those empty conceited Fellows, who repeat as Sayings of their own, or some of their particular Friends, several Jests which were made before they were born ... Upon the reading of them, he was under no small Confusion to find that all his Jokes had passed through several Editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming or repeating familiar/well-circulated jokes as original material. Remedy: read collections and common sources (the author recommends jest-books) to learn provenance and prevent unconscious repetition; this improves originality and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sincerity to polite falsehood in character and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth they call Barbarity, and Falsehood Politeness. (From the Ambassador of Bantam's letter describing a people who say one thing and mean another.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying social behaviour or crafting comedic situations, expose hypocrisy and insincerity rather than endorsing flattery. The essay uses concrete comic examples (insincere condolences, overdone apologies, false offers of service) to satirize polite falsehoods; valuing frankness yields clearer moral and comic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and personification to dramatize moral lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: A vision: Jupiter proclaims that every Mortal should bring in his Griefs and Calamities... Fancy carries a magnifying Glass... afterwards Patience returns every Man his own proper Calamity, and teaching him how to bear it...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid allegorical scenes (personified abstractions like Fancy, Patience, a Mountain of Miseries) to make ethical points memorable and entertaining. Structural devices — a spectacular conceit, an imagined public scene, followed by a reversal or lesson — effectively combine humour with moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid, concrete characterization and ironic detail in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The Widow-Club: nine particular dames with detailed, comic biographies (Mrs. President, Mrs. Snapp, Mrs. Medlar, etc.) and particular club rules about managing husbands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire gains force from specific, memorable particulars: named characters, curious particulars (ages, habits, marital histories), club rules, and ironic institutional details. Concrete lists and exaggerated yet plausible traits make social types recognizable and amusing.
